name: Grade 2
theme: Forgiveness and the Eucharist: preparing for first sacraments

lessons.title: Made in God’s image
lessons.idea: God made us with a body and a soul. We can think, choose and love. This makes us different from the animals.
lessons.question: What can people do that animals cannot?
lessons.activity: Draw a self-portrait and list three gifts God gave you.
teach: We have a body and a soul. The soul lives forever (CCC 362–366). We can think, choose and love.
We are made in God’s image (Genesis 1:26–27; CCC 355).
Celebrate differences: everyone is made in God’s image.
talk: What can you do that your pet cannot?
How can you take care of your body and your soul?
quiz: People are made of…|Body and soul|Only body|Only soul|Clay only|0|CCC 362.
The soul…|Dies with the body|Lives forever|Is a feeling|Is a thought|1|CCC 366.
We are made in God’s…|Shadow|Image|House|Costume|1|Genesis 1:27.
lessons.life: Thank God each morning for your body and your soul.
lessons.saint: Francis de Sales: he taught that a happy heart honors God.
lessons.mem: God made me in his image. (Genesis 1:27)
lessons.hook: Look in a mirror. Ask, “What can you do that a dog can’t?”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What are two gifts God gave you?”

script.open: Show a mirror and a photograph. Ask, “Which one looks more like you? The mirror shows you right now. The photo shows how you looked once. Today we will learn about a picture that is even more special: the picture of God that is inside every person.”
teach: Read Genesis 1:26-27: “Then God said, ‘Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.’ So God created man in his own image.” Say: “An image is a picture or a likeness. Does this mean God has a body like ours? No. God is a spirit. It means we are like God in the important ways: we can think, choose and love.”

Say: “Animals are good, and God loves them. But animals cannot pray, or tell right from wrong, or choose to love someone forever. We can. God gave us a soul, which is the invisible part of us that never dies. Your soul is why you are a person, and not just a clever animal. Your body and your soul together are you.”

Say: “Psalm 8 says: ‘You have made them a little lower than the angels and crowned them with glory and honor.’ Every person, from the tiniest baby to the oldest grandparent, is made in God’s image. That means every person is precious. We must treat them with respect.”
ask: What is a soul? (The invisible part of us that lives forever.)
What can people do that animals cannot? (Pray, love God, choose, know right from wrong.)
Why should we respect every person? (Everyone is made in God’s image.)
practice: Give each child a sheet divided in two: a self-portrait on one side, and three boxes on the other.
Say: “Draw yourself. Then think of three gifts God gave you. They can be things you can do, or things about you, like a kind heart or a strong voice.”
Walk around and help children name their gifts.
Invite each child to share one gift with a partner, and the partner says, “God gave you a good gift.”
script.close: Pray: “God, thank you for making me in your image.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell your family one gift you saw in each person.”

tryit: Write three gifts God gave you.
lessons.saintStory:
Francis de Sales was born in 1567 in the French Alps, into a noble family. He became a priest and then bishop of Geneva, a city where most people did not welcome Catholics.
Bishop Francis was known for being gentle. He used to say that you catch more flies with a spoonful of honey than with a barrel of vinegar. He wrote notes and leaflets, pushed under doors, to explain the faith kindly, and he wrote a book to help ordinary people become holy in daily life, not just monks and nuns.
Francis taught that a cheerful, patient heart honors God, because God made us with joy. He shows us that being made in God’s image means we can be kind, thoughtful and happy.

lessons.title: Free to choose
lessons.idea: God gave us free will. We can choose good or evil. When we choose good, we grow in goodness.
lessons.question: What is a good choice you made this week?
lessons.activity: Sort “good choice” and “bad choice” cards and explain why.
teach: Free will lets us choose good or evil (CCC 1730–1731). God wants us to choose love freely.
Deuteronomy 30:19: “Choose life.”
Link choices to growing in goodness.
talk: What good choice did you make this week?
quiz: Free will lets us…|Be forced|Choose|Hide|Forget|1|CCC 1731.
Good choices lead to…|Nothing|Happiness and goodness|Sadness|Trouble|1|CCC 1733.
Who helps us choose well?|Nobody|God, family, the Church|Only a screen|Only friends|1|CCC 1783.
lessons.life: Before you decide something this week, say a quick prayer: “Jesus, help me choose well.”
lessons.saint: Aloysius Gonzaga: he chose to give up his inheritance to serve God.
lessons.mem: Choose life. (Deuteronomy 30:19)
lessons.hook: Hold two paths drawn on paper. “You choose which way.”
lessons.assess: Ask for an example of a good choice and a bad choice.

script.open: Put two paths on the floor with masking tape, one marked with a smiley heart, the other with a frowny face. Say, “Every day we walk on one of these two paths. Whenever you have to choose, you pick one. Today we will talk about the power to choose.”
teach: Say: “God made us with free will. That means we can choose. Nobody can force us to love. You can say yes or no. God did not make us like robots, who can only do what they are told. He wants us to love him freely, from our hearts.”

Read Deuteronomy 30:19: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Choose life.” Say: “Moses told the people to choose. When we choose good things, we grow in goodness. It is like practicing piano: the more we practice, the better we get.”

Say: “When we choose bad things, it hurts us and others. That is sin. But God never takes our freedom away. He helps us to choose well. He gives us a conscience, the Church’s teachings, and good people to help us. And when we fail, he forgives.”
ask: What is free will? (The power to choose.)
What happens when we choose good things? (We grow in goodness and are happy.)
Who helps us choose well? (God, our conscience, our parents, the Church.)
practice: Prepare cards with choices: “share a toy,” “tell the truth,” “hit your brother,” “say thank you,” “take something that is not yours,” “pray before bed.”
Spread two mats: “good choice” and “not-good choice.”
Let each child draw a card, read it with help, and put it on the right mat. Ask, “Why?”
Take a “not-good” card and say, “What could we choose instead?”
script.close: Pray: “God, help me to choose good.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Make one good choice and notice how it feels.”

tryit: Sort the cards into good and not-good choices.
Choose one good thing to do today.
lessons.saintStory:
Aloysius Gonzaga was born in 1568 in northern Italy. His father was a marquis, and he was supposed to become a soldier and a lord. He grew up in a palace, but he wanted something different. He loved to pray, and he decided to become a priest.
His father did not want it, and argued with Aloysius for a long time. Aloysius gave up his right to his father’s lands and titles, and joined the Jesuits in Rome when he was seventeen. Later, when a plague came to Rome, Aloysius helped to carry the sick into the hospital and care for them. He caught the sickness himself and died at twenty-three.
Aloysius made the choices that were hard, but good. He shows that using our freedom to love God makes us truly free.

lessons.title: Sin hurts and God heals
lessons.idea: Sin hurts our friendship with God and others. God never stops loving us. He sent Jesus to save us.
lessons.question: How did the father welcome the son?
lessons.activity: Act out the Prodigal Son. Say, “Welcome home.”
teach: Sin hurts our friendship with God and others (CCC 1846, 1850). God never stops loving us.
The Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32): the father runs to welcome his son.
Emphasize mercy first.
talk: How did the father welcome his son?
What does God do when we come home?
quiz: The father in the story…|Ran to welcome his son|Closed the door|Scolded him|Sent him away|0|Luke 15:20.
The father is like…|God|A judge|A stranger|A teacher|0|CCC 1439.
Sin hurts…|Only us|Nobody|Only teachers|Our friendship with God and others|3|CCC 1850.
lessons.life: If you did something wrong this week, say, “I’m sorry” to the person and to God.
lessons.saint: Augustine: a young man who ran away from God, and came home.
lessons.mem: My child, you are always with me. (Luke 15:31)
lessons.hook: Tell about a friend who was hurt. “What would make it right?”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What did the father do?”

script.open: Show a house key, and ask, “What would it be like to be locked out of your house? Today’s story is about a boy who left his father’s house and then found his way back.”
teach: Tell Luke 15: “A father had two sons. The younger one said, ‘Father, give me my share of the money.’ He went far away and spent it all on silly things. Soon he was poor and hungry, feeding pigs. He thought, ‘My father’s workers have food. I will go home and say, I have sinned. I am not worthy to be called your son.’”

Say: “But while he was still far away, his father saw him. His father ran to him, hugged him and kissed him. The son said, ‘Father, I have sinned.’ The father said to his servants, ‘Bring the best robe, put a ring on his finger, and kill the calf. We will celebrate! My son was dead and is alive. He was lost and is found.’”

Say: “Sin hurts. It hurts our friendship with God and with other people. It makes us feel far away. But the father in the story is like God. He does not stop loving us. He runs to meet us. He sent Jesus to bring us home, and every time we say sorry, he welcomes us back.”
ask: What did the younger son do wrong? (He left, and wasted what he was given.)
What did the father do when he saw him? (He ran, hugged him, and had a party.)
Who is the father like? (God.) What does he do when we are sorry? (Forgives us.)
practice: Choose children to be the father, the younger son, the older brother and the servants.
Act out the story: the son leaves, runs out of money, comes back, and the father runs to hug him.
The father says, “Welcome home!” and the son says, “I am sorry.”
Switch roles so several children get to be the son and father.
script.close: Pray the Act of Contrition: “O my God, I am sorry for my sins.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Give someone a ‘welcome home’ hug.”

tryit: Act out the story of the son who came home.
lessons.saintStory:
Augustine was born in North Africa in the year 354. He was very clever and did well in school, but he did not want to obey. As a young man he lived wildly, and he cared more about being famous than about being good.
His mother, Monica, prayed for him every day. Augustine went to Italy. One day in a garden he heard a child’s voice singing, “Take and read, take and read.” He picked up the Bible, read a verse, and felt his heart change. He was baptized at thirty-two. He later became a bishop and wrote many books.
Augustine wrote, “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” His story is like the story of the Prodigal Son, because God always welcomes us home.

units.title: Jesus teaches us
units.eq: How does Jesus teach us to live?

lessons.title: The Good Shepherd
lessons.idea: Jesus is the Good Shepherd who knows us and cares for us. He leads us to the Father.
lessons.question: What does a shepherd do for the sheep?
lessons.activity: Make a sheep from cotton balls. Pray Psalm 23 together.
teach: Jesus is the Good Shepherd who knows and loves us (John 10:11–16; CCC 754). He leads us to the Father.
Psalm 23 is a prayer of trust.
Gentle voice.
talk: How does a shepherd care for sheep?
What does it feel like to be known by name?
How does Jesus care for you?
quiz: The Good Shepherd is…|Peter|Noah|Moses|Jesus|3|John 10:11.
The Shepherd knows…|Only the lost|Only some|His sheep by name|No one|2|John 10:3.
Psalm 23 says “The Lord is my…”|King|Teacher|Friend|Shepherd|3|Psalm 23:1.
lessons.life: Pray Psalm 23 before bed this week.
lessons.saint: John XXIII: a farm boy who became the “Good Pope,” a shepherd loved by everyone.
lessons.mem: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. (Psalm 23:1)
lessons.hook: Hold a toy sheep. “A shepherd knows his sheep by name.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to say the first line of Psalm 23.

script.open: Bring a stuffed lamb or cotton ball sheep. Ask, “What does a shepherd do? How does he look after sheep?” Let children share ideas: feed them, find water, protect from wolves, find lost ones.
teach: Read John 10:11-14 slowly: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep… I know my sheep and my sheep know me.” Say: “Jesus says he is the Good Shepherd. We are his sheep. A good shepherd knows each sheep by name and takes care of each one.”

Say: “Jesus is a very good shepherd. He knows you. He knows what you need. He leads you the right way. He protects you. And he loved us so much that he gave his life for us, on the cross. And he rose again.”

Read Psalm 23 together, line by line, with the children repeating. Say: “‘The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul.’ Even in the dark valley, the shepherd is with us.”
ask: Who is the Good Shepherd? (Jesus.) Who are the sheep? (We are.)
What does a good shepherd do? (Knows us, protects us, finds us when lost.)
What does Psalm 23 say about the shepherd? (He is with us, even in dark times.)
practice: Give each child a paper outline of a sheep and cotton balls, glue and a crayon.
Help each child glue cotton balls on the outline for the wool.
As they work, pray Psalm 23 one line at a time. Children repeat each line.
Write the child’s name on the sheep, and say: “Jesus knows you by name.”
script.close: Pray Psalm 23 together once more. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray Psalm 23 at bedtime.”

lessons.saintStory:
Angelo Roncalli was born in 1881 in a poor farming family in northern Italy, one of thirteen children. He went to seminary as a boy, became a priest, and then served the Church around the world, in Bulgaria, Turkey and France.
In 1958 he was elected pope and took the name John XXIII. People called him “the good Pope.” He was round, jolly and kind. He visited children in the hospital and prisoners in jail, and he said to the prisoners, “You could not come to me, so I came to you.” In 1962 he opened the Second Vatican Council, a big meeting of bishops from all over the world.
Pope John was like a good shepherd who cares for his sheep. He shows what Jesus the Good Shepherd is like.

lessons.title: Parables of the kingdom
lessons.idea: Jesus told stories to help us know God’s kingdom. The mustard seed and the lost sheep show God’s love.
lessons.question: What do the parables teach us about God?
lessons.activity: Retell the parable of the lost sheep with props.
teach: A parable is a story with a hidden meaning (CCC 546). Mustard seed: the Kingdom starts small and grows (Matthew 13:31–32).
The lost sheep shows God’s love for each one (Luke 15:1–7).
Let children retell stories.
talk: Why did the shepherd leave the 99?
How did he feel when he found the sheep?
Who is the shepherd in your life?
quiz: A parable is…|A prayer|A song|A trick|A story Jesus told|3|CCC 546.
The lost sheep teaches us that God…|Forgets|Searches for us|Is angry|Hides|1|Luke 15:4-7.
The mustard seed is…|Large|Small but grows big|A tree|Useless|1|Matthew 13:31-32.
lessons.life: Look for a way to help someone who feels lost or left out.
lessons.saint: Josephine Bakhita: a girl who was lost and found, and who knew God’s love.
misc: “The Kingdom is a place on a map.”
lessons.mem: The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed. (Matthew 13:31)
lessons.hook: Show a tiny seed. “What could it become?”
lessons.assess: Ask children to retell one parable.

script.open: Hide a small object, such as a coin, in the room before class begins. Say, “I lost something. I will keep looking until I find it. How would you feel if you found it?” Let children help look for it. Celebrate when it is found.
teach: Say: “Jesus often told stories to teach about the kingdom of God. The kingdom means God’s rule of love. Stories like this are called parables. They are small stories about everyday things, like sheep, coins and seeds, with a big meaning.”

Tell Luke 15:1-7: “A shepherd had one hundred sheep. One got lost. He left the ninety-nine, and he went to look for the one. When he found it, he put it on his shoulders and went home rejoicing. He told his friends, ‘Rejoice with me, I found my sheep!’ Jesus says there is more joy in heaven over one person who comes back to God than over ninety-nine who never got lost. God is like that shepherd. He never stops looking for us.”

Tell Matthew 13:31-32: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds. But when it grows, it becomes a tall bush, big enough for birds to build nests in it.” Say: “God’s kingdom starts small, in our hearts, and grows. Every small kindness grows.”
ask: Who is the shepherd in the story? (Jesus, or God.)
How does God feel when someone comes back to him? (Very happy.)
What is something small that grows into something big? (A seed, a kindness, a friendship.)
practice: Use a sheep toy, a hill of cloth and a few other sheep (or cotton balls).
Retell the story while children move the pieces: the shepherd leaves, finds the sheep, brings it home.
Show a mustard seed (or a tiny seed) in the palm of your hand, and a picture of a big mustard bush.
Plant the seed in a cup with soil together.
script.close: Pray: “Thank you, Jesus, for looking for us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell your family the story of the lost sheep.”

tryit: Act out the lost sheep with props.
lessons.saintStory:
Bakhita was born in Sudan in about 1869. When she was around seven or nine, she was kidnapped by slave traders and taken far from her family. She was so frightened that she forgot her own name. The traders called her “Bakhita,” which means “lucky,” and that is the name she is known by.
She was bought and sold, and treated cruelly, until she was taken to Italy. There she met the Canossian Sisters and learned about God. She said she had always known there was a Lord who made everything and loved her. She was baptized, set free by an Italian court, and became a sister.
Sister Josephine was kind and gentle for many years. She said, “The Lord has loved me so much.” She shows us that Jesus is the shepherd who looks for lost sheep.

lessons.title: The Beatitudes
lessons.idea: Jesus gave us eight ways to be happy. Following them leads us to God.
lessons.question: Which Beatitude is hardest for you?
lessons.activity: Make an eight-sided Beatitudes poster with child-friendly words.
teach: The Beatitudes are Jesus’ ways to be happy (Matthew 5:1–12; CCC 1716–1718).
Child-friendly: happy are those who are kind, who share, who make peace.
Let children illustrate one.
talk: Which Beatitude is easiest for you?
Who in your life lives these?
quiz: The Beatitudes begin with…|Blessed|Beware|Because|Be quiet|0|Matthew 5:3.
Blessed means…|Happy with God|Rich|Famous|Strong|0|CCC 1716.
The Beatitudes were taught on…|A boat|A house|A road|A mountain|3|Matthew 5:1.
lessons.life: Pick one Beatitude to try this week and note what happens.
lessons.saint: Clare of Assisi: a girl from a rich family who chose to be poor in spirit for Jesus.
lessons.mem: Blessed are the peacemakers. (Matthew 5:9)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What makes you happy?” List their answers.
lessons.assess: Ask children to choose one Beatitude and say what it means.

script.open: Say, “What makes someone really happy? Let’s make a list on the board.” Write what the children say (toys, candy, friends, a pet, family). “Now we will hear what Jesus says makes us really happy.”
teach: Say: “Jesus went up on a mountain, sat down, and taught the people. He gave us eight special ways to be happy, which we call the Beatitudes. The word beatitude means ‘blessed’ or ‘happy.’ They are in Matthew 5.”

Read them in child-friendly words: “Happy are those who know they need God. Happy are those who are sad, for God will comfort them. Happy are the gentle. Happy are those who want to do what is right. Happy are those who show mercy. Happy are the pure of heart. Happy are the peacemakers. Happy are those who are treated badly for doing good.” Pause after each one for children to say what it means.

Say: “Jesus says the way to be truly happy is not to have lots of things, or to be the strongest. It is to love God and other people. This is a surprise! But it is true. Following the Beatitudes leads us to God, and to heaven. They are like a map to happiness.”
ask: What does ‘beatitude’ mean? (Blessed, happy.)
Which one is about making peace? (Blessed are the peacemakers.) How can you be a peacemaker? (Stop a fight, say sorry, share.)
Which one do you want to try this week? (Let children choose.)
practice: Draw an octagon (eight sides) on a large paper, or give each child a paper plate with eight sections.
Help the class write a child-friendly version of one Beatitude in each section: “Be gentle,” “Make peace,” “Be kind,” “Say sorry.”
Let the children illustrate each section.
Display the poster. Choose one to live this week.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, help us live the Beatitudes.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Live one Beatitude and tell us about it.”

tryit: Make a poster with child-friendly words.
Choose one to live this week.
lessons.saintStory:
Clare was born in Assisi, Italy, in 1194 to a rich and noble family. When she was a girl, she heard Francis, a young man from her town, preach about following Jesus in poverty and joy. She wanted this too.
When she was eighteen, Clare left her family’s home one night and met Francis and his friends at a little chapel. They cut her hair, and she put on a rough dress. She went to live at the church of San Damiano with the other women who joined her, called the Poor Clares. They lived very simply, praying and working.
Clare was joyful. She said that the poor in spirit, those who did not need riches, were the happiest. She shows us what the Beatitudes look like.

lessons.title: Conscience: our inner guide
lessons.idea: Conscience helps us know right from wrong. We should listen to it and form it with the Church’s teaching.
lessons.question: How do you know something is wrong?
lessons.activity: Make “stop and think” cards with questions to ask before acting.
teach: Conscience is God’s voice helping us know good from evil (Romans 2:14–15; CCC 1776–1777, 1783). It must be trained.
Ask: Is this kind? Is this true? Is this safe?
Do not frighten; a conscience guides us.
talk: How do you know right from wrong?
What do you feel when you do wrong?
quiz: Conscience is…|A friend|A teacher|An inner voice that helps us know right from wrong|A feeling only|2|CCC 1776.
We should…|Ignore it|Follow our conscience and learn what is good|Argue|Hide|1|CCC 1783.
To form conscience, we…|Hide|Guess|Pray and learn|Fight|2|CCC 1785.
lessons.life: Ask “Is this loving?” before you act.
lessons.saint: Joan of Arc: a young woman who followed her conscience, even when it was hard.
lessons.mem: Help me do what is right, Lord.
lessons.hook: Say, “Have you ever felt a little voice saying ‘don’t do that’?”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What do you do when your conscience says stop?”

script.open: Show a traffic light with red, yellow and green circles. Ask, “What does each color mean? What do we do?” Take answers. “Today we will learn about a light inside us that helps us choose.”
teach: Say: “Inside each of us there is a quiet voice that tells us if something is right or wrong. It is called conscience. When you take a cookie that is not yours, you feel a little sad. That is your conscience. When you share something, you feel happy. That is your conscience, too. God put it in our hearts.”
Read Romans 2:15: “They show that what the law requires is written on their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness.” Say: “God’s law is written in our hearts.”

Say: “Our conscience needs to be trained, like a muscle. We learn from our parents, teachers, the Bible, the Ten Commandments and the Church. We should listen to it, and ask God to help us choose well. Before we choose, we can ask: Is this kind? Is this true? Would Jesus do this? If we are not sure, we ask someone wise.”
ask: What is conscience? (A voice inside that tells us right from wrong.)
Who gave us a conscience? (God.)
Who helps us learn what is right? (Parents, teachers, the Church, the Bible.)
practice: Give each child an index card or a paper circle.
Say: “This is your ‘stop and think’ card. We will write three questions on it.” Write them together: “Is it kind?” “Is it true?” “Would Jesus do it?”
Let children decorate the card with a red, yellow and green circle.
Practice with a scenario: “Your friend wants you to copy his homework.” Hold up the card and ask the questions out loud.
script.close: Pray: “Holy Spirit, help me do what is right.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Use your card when you need to choose.”

lessons.saintStory:
Joan was born in 1412 in a small village in France. Her family was poor and she was a farm girl. When she was about thirteen, she said she began to hear the voices of saints, who told her to help save France, which was at war.
At seventeen she dressed as a soldier and went to the king. She inspired the army and helped lift the siege of the city of Orléans. The French king was crowned. But later she was captured and put on trial. The judges tried to trick her. They wanted her to say that her voices had not come from God. She refused to say what she knew was not true.
Joan was put to death at nineteen. Later the Church declared her innocent, and then a saint. She shows us what it means to follow your conscience, even when it is hard.

lessons.title: Examining our hearts
lessons.idea: Before Confession we think about what we did and ask God for help. We remember: did I love God, my family and others?
lessons.question: What happens when we do not tell the truth?
lessons.activity: Practice an age-appropriate examination of conscience with prompts.
teach: Before Confession we look at our hearts (Psalm 139:23–24; CCC 1454–1455). Ask: Did I love God? My family? Others?
Use three or four simple questions.
End with God’s mercy.
quiz: An examination of conscience helps us…|Judge others|Remember how we loved|Hide|Count candy|1|CCC 1454.
Before Confession we…|Run|Hide|Eat|Think and pray|3|CCC 1454.
We are sorry because…|It is a rule|We love God|We were caught|We are afraid|1|CCC 1451.
lessons.life: Before bed, think of one good thing and one thing you want to do better.
lessons.saint: Ignatius of Loyola: he taught an evening examen.
lessons.mem: Search me, O God, and know my heart. (Psalm 139:23)
lessons.hook: Hold a flashlight. “We shine a light inside our hearts.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to answer two examination questions.

script.open: Play a short ‘rewind’ game: ask the children to close their eyes and think about what they did this morning, one thing at a time. Then say, “Now we’ve looked back on the morning. We will learn to look back on our lives with God’s help.”
teach: Say: “Before we go to Confession, we think about what we did. This is called an examination of conscience. To examine means to look closely. We look at our hearts in God’s light. We ask the Holy Spirit to help us see clearly.”

Read Psalm 139:23-24: “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! See if there is any hurtful way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.” Say: “This is a good prayer to say first.”

Say: “We can ask these questions: Did I love God? Did I pray? Did I obey my parents and teachers? Was I kind to my family and friends? Did I tell the truth? Did I share? Did I take something that was not mine? Did I say unkind words? Did I do something I knew was wrong? We are not looking for ways to feel bad. We are looking so that we can say sorry and start fresh.”
ask: What does ‘examine’ mean? (Look closely.)
Why do we examine our conscience before Confession? (So that we know what to say sorry for.)
What do we do after we think about our sins? (Tell them in Confession and say sorry.)
practice: Light a candle. Have children sit quietly with hands folded.
Say, “Let’s ask the Holy Spirit to help us.” Pray, “Come, Holy Spirit.”
Read out the questions slowly, one at a time, and pause for twenty seconds after each so children can think.
After the last question, pray the Act of Contrition together.
script.close: Say the Act of Contrition one more time. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look back on your day tonight, and say sorry and thank you to God.”

lessons.saintStory:
Ignatius was born in 1491 in the Basque country of Spain. He grew up as a nobleman and a soldier, and he cared about fame and glory. In 1521 a cannonball struck his leg in a battle, and he had to rest for a long time in bed.
There were no adventure books at hand, only books about Jesus and the saints. He read them, and he began to think, “What if I did what the saints did?” He noticed that thinking about worldly things made him feel empty, and thinking about God left him joyful. He learned to pay attention to what was happening inside him.
Ignatius became a priest and began the Jesuits. He taught a simple way of ending the day by looking back at it with God. It is called the Examen. It is a good way to prepare for Confession.

lessons.title: The sacrament of Reconciliation
lessons.idea: We tell our sins to a priest. He gives us a penance and forgives us in Jesus’ name. We feel God’s peace.
lessons.question: What does the priest say after Confession?
lessons.activity: Walk through the steps of Confession using cards. Practice the Act of Contrition.
teach: Steps: greet, Sign of the Cross, “Bless me, Father, for I have sinned,” tell sins, listen, Act of Contrition, absolution, penance (CCC 1450, 1455, 1480).
The priest cannot tell anyone (the seal).
Practice with an adult play-acting.
talk: What do you say at the beginning?
What penance might the priest give?
quiz: Who forgives in Confession?|Nobody|God, through the priest|A friend|The priest alone|1|CCC 1461.
The priest says the words of…|Thanks|Greetings|Goodbye|Absolution|3|CCC 1449.
Confession is private because of…|Embarrassment|The seal|Habit|A rule of school|1|CCC 1467.
lessons.life: Practice the Act of Contrition each night.
lessons.saint: Leopold Mandić: a very small priest who heard confessions for many hours every day.
lessons.mem: O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended you.
lessons.hook: Show the steps on cards. “Let’s practice so it feels easy.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to name the steps in order.

script.open: Show a small jar of clean water and a jar of muddy water. “What is the difference? Which would you want to drink? When we sin, it is like mud in our hearts. Confession is how God cleans us.”
teach: Read John 20:21-23: “Jesus said to them again, ‘Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.’ And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven.’” Say: “Jesus gave his friends the power to forgive sins in his name. That is why we go to a priest. The priest acts in the name of Jesus.”

Walk through the steps with cards, one at a time: “1. Make the Sign of the Cross. The priest welcomes you. 2. Say, ‘Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. This is my first Confession.’ 3. Tell your sins. 4. Listen to the priest’s advice. 5. He gives you a penance, a prayer or an act of kindness. 6. Say the Act of Contrition. 7. The priest says the words of forgiveness: ‘I absolve you from your sins, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’ 8. He says, ‘Go in peace.’ You say, ‘Thanks be to God.’”
Say: “Everything you say is a secret. The priest can never tell anyone. Confession is a gift. When it is finished, you will feel light and free.”
ask: Who gave priests the power to forgive sins? (Jesus.)
What do you say first in Confession? (Bless me, Father, for I have sinned.)
What does the priest do at the end? (Gives words of forgiveness, ‘I absolve you.’)
practice: Lay out the eight step cards in a line on the floor.
Mix them up, then have children put them in order and say what happens.
Practice with a pretend confessional: two children, one as the priest and one as the child.
Practice the Act of Contrition aloud together, as many times as needed.
script.close: Say the Act of Contrition. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask your parents when we can go to Confession.”

tryit: Walk through the steps of Confession.
lessons.saintStory:
Leopold Mandić was born in 1866 in a part of Croatia, and as a boy he was very small and had trouble speaking. He grew to be only about four feet five inches tall. He joined the Capuchins and wanted to be a missionary to the people of the East, but his health and his stutter made that impossible.
Instead he spent more than thirty years in the city of Padua in Italy, mostly in a tiny room, hearing confessions. People came from all over to see him, because he was so kind and understanding. He would sit up to fifteen hours a day. He told the people he forgave, “Take courage. I will take part of your penance on myself.”
Leopold shows that God’s mercy is great, and a kind priest helps us meet it. He died in 1942.

units.title: Preparing for the Eucharist
units.eq: Who do we receive in Communion?

lessons.title: The Last Supper
lessons.idea: Jesus gave us the Eucharist at the Last Supper. He changed bread and wine into his Body and Blood.
lessons.question: What did Jesus do at the Last Supper?
lessons.activity: Set a simple table. Retell the story with bread and a cup.
teach: At the Last Supper Jesus gave us the Eucharist (Luke 22:14–20; CCC 1337, 1339–1340). He said, “Do this in memory of me.”
Every Mass remembers and makes present the Last Supper and the Cross.
Use reverent actions.
talk: What did Jesus say over the bread?
quiz: At the Last Supper Jesus gave…|A song|His Body and Blood|A map|A speech|1|Luke 22:19.
Jesus said, “Do this in…”|Secret|Memory of me|The morning|Your house|1|Luke 22:19.
The Eucharist means…|Party|Thanksgiving|Lunch|Dinner|1|CCC 1328.
lessons.life: At Mass, listen for the words of Jesus over the bread and wine.
lessons.saint: Thomas Aquinas: wrote hymns to the Eucharist.
lessons.mem: This is my body. This is my blood. (see Luke 22:19–20)
lessons.hook: Set a table with bread and a cup. “Jesus shared a special meal with his friends.”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What did Jesus do at the Last Supper?”

script.open: Set a table with a white cloth, a candle, a loaf of bread, a cup of juice and a plate. Ask the children to sit around it. Say, “This is a special meal. Let me tell you about a very special meal, the night before Jesus died.”
teach: Tell Luke 22:14-20: “It was Thursday night, the night before Jesus died. He sat at a table with his twelve friends, the apostles, to eat the Passover meal. Jesus took bread. He gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, ‘This is my body, which is given for you.’ Then he took the cup of wine and said, ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this in memory of me.’”

Say: “That meal is called the Last Supper. Jesus gave us the Eucharist, the greatest gift. He changed bread and wine into his Body and Blood. And he told his apostles, ‘Do this in memory of me.’ That means: Keep doing this. That is why every priest, at every Mass, does what Jesus did.”

Say: “The word Eucharist means ‘thanksgiving.’ At Mass we give thanks to God for all he has given us, especially Jesus. We go to Mass on Sunday to be with Jesus, and to receive him in Holy Communion.”
ask: What happened at the Last Supper? (Jesus gave us the Eucharist.)
What did Jesus say about the bread? (This is my body.)
What does ‘Eucharist’ mean? (Thanksgiving.)
practice: Seat the children around the table. Let one child play Jesus (or you).
Retell the story while the children pass the bread and cup around (a small piece for each, just for the story).
Say the words slowly: “Take and eat.” Make it quiet and reverent.
Afterward say, “Thank you, Jesus, for the Eucharist.”
script.close: Pray the first lines of Tantum Ergo or say: “Jesus, we adore you in the Eucharist.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “At Mass, listen for the words of Jesus the priest says.”

tryit: Retell the Last Supper with bread and a cup.
lessons.saintStory:
Thomas was born in 1225 in Italy, to a noble family. His family wanted him to be a rich abbot, but he wanted to join the Dominicans, who were poor friars. His brothers locked him up for a year, but he would not give up.
Thomas was a quiet and enormous man. His classmates called him “the Dumb Ox,” but his teacher said that the bellowing of this ox would be heard all over the world. He studied and wrote and taught, and became one of the greatest teachers in Church history. His big book, the Summa Theologiae, explains the faith.
The Church asked Thomas to write the prayers and hymns for a new feast, Corpus Christi, the Body of Christ. He wrote songs such as “Tantum Ergo,” which we still sing. Thomas shows how much a saint loved the Eucharist.

lessons.title: Jesus is truly present
lessons.idea: After the priest says the words, bread and wine become Jesus. We call this the Real Presence.
lessons.question: How do we show respect to Jesus in the Eucharist?
lessons.activity: Practice reverent reception, hands and genuflections.
teach: The Real Presence: Jesus is truly there, body, blood, soul and divinity (CCC 1374–1376). Teach slowly.
John 6:51: “I am the living bread.”
Practice reverent reception.
talk: What do you say to Jesus?
quiz: After the consecration, the bread is…|Jesus|Still only bread|A cookie|A symbol|0|CCC 1374.
We call this presence…|Shadow|Pretend|Real Presence|Fake|2|CCC 1374.
We receive Jesus in…|A book|A prayer|A song|Holy Communion|3|CCC 1391.
lessons.life: Make a quiet visit to the church this week and say “Jesus, I believe you are here.”
lessons.saint: Paschal Baylon: a shepherd boy who grew up to love Jesus in the Eucharist.
lessons.mem: Jesus, I believe you are here.
lessons.hook: Hold bread. “How can this be Jesus? We believe because he said so.”
lessons.assess: Ask: “Who is in the Eucharist?”

script.open: Show a picture of a monstrance with the Eucharist in it, and a picture of an ordinary piece of bread. Say, “They look the same. But there is a very big difference. Today we are going to find out what it is.”
teach: Say: “Remember the Last Supper? Jesus said, ‘This is my body.’ At every Mass, the priest says the words of Jesus. After he says, ‘This is my body,’ the bread is not bread anymore. It becomes the Body of Jesus. It still looks like bread, tastes like bread. But it is Jesus. The wine becomes his Blood. We call this the Real Presence.”

Read John 6:51-55 in simple words: “Jesus said, ‘I am the living bread. Whoever eats this bread will live forever. The bread that I will give is my flesh.’ Many people could not believe it. But Jesus said it again. For him, it is true.”

Say: “That is why we are so quiet and respectful at Mass. It is why we genuflect to the tabernacle. And why we prepare our hearts before Holy Communion. Jesus is really there. When we receive Communion, we receive Jesus himself. He comes to live in us.”
ask: What does the bread become at Mass? (The Body of Jesus.)
Does it look different? (No. It still looks like bread.)
How do we show respect for Jesus? (Quiet, genuflect, fold hands, receive reverently.)
practice: Practice walking to Communion with folded hands, slowly and quietly.
Show how to receive in the hand (left hand over right, palm up, like a throne) or on the tongue. Say “Amen” after the priest says “The Body of Christ.”
Practice genuflecting: right knee to the floor.
End with a quiet whisper: “Jesus, I believe you are here.”
script.close: Whisper the prayer together: “Jesus, I believe you are here.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “At Mass, whisper that prayer when you see the priest lift the Host.”

tryit: Whisper: “Jesus, I believe you are here.”
lessons.saintStory:
Paschal Baylon was born in 1540 in Spain, to a poor farming family. As a boy he looked after sheep on the hills. He couldn’t read, so he asked other shepherds to teach him, and he carried a little book of prayers in his pocket, and read it whenever he could.
When he grew up, he joined the Franciscans as a lay brother. He worked as the porter, the person who answered the door of the monastery. He was kind to everyone who came, especially the poor. And he loved to pray in front of the Eucharist, for hours at a time. Sometimes people said they saw him lost in deep prayer.
Paschal is called the patron of Eucharistic congresses. He shows us that Jesus is truly present in the Eucharist, and wants to be with us.

lessons.title: The parts of the Mass
lessons.idea: The Mass has four parts: gathering, God’s word, the Eucharist and sending forth.
lessons.question: What do we do at each part of Mass?
lessons.activity: Order cards of the Mass, then play a “what comes next” game.
teach: Four parts: gathering, God’s word, the Eucharist, sending forth (CCC 1346, 1348–1355). Link to Emmaus (Luke 24).
Practice responses: “Thanks be to God.”
Take children on a church tour.
quiz: Mass begins with…|The Entrance|Communion|The sermon|The blessing|0|CCC 1348.
We hear readings in…|The Dismissal|The Preface|The Liturgy of the Word|Communion|2|CCC 1349.
Mass ends with…|The Gospel|The blessing and dismissal|The Creed|The Gloria|1|CCC 1332.
lessons.life: Use the Mass mode with your family at Mass this week.
lessons.saint: Cyril of Jerusalem: a bishop who explained the Mass to new Christians.
lessons.mem: Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Lord, have mercy.
lessons.hook: Lay out cards of the four parts. “Mass has a shape.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to arrange the parts of Mass.

script.open: Lay out a very simple jigsaw puzzle, with a few large pieces, and let a pair of children assemble it. Say, “What happens if one piece is missing? Today we will see the four big pieces of the Mass.”
teach: Say: “The Mass is a prayer with four big parts, like four rooms in a house. Part one: The Introductory Rites, when we gather. We come in, sing, make the Sign of the Cross, and say sorry for our sins. We say, ‘Lord, have mercy.’”

Say: “Part two: the Liturgy of the Word, when we listen to God. We hear readings from the Bible, sing a psalm, stand for the Gospel. The priest gives a homily, and we pray for the Church and the world. Part three: the Liturgy of the Eucharist. The priest takes bread and wine, and says the words of Jesus. They become Jesus’ Body and Blood. We pray the Our Father, and receive Communion.”

Say: “Part four: the Concluding Rites, when we are sent out. The priest blesses us and says, ‘Go in peace.’ We answer, ‘Thanks be to God.’ And we go out to share Jesus’ love. The Mass is like the story of the two friends on the road to Emmaus: God speaks, Jesus breaks bread, and our hearts burn within us.”
ask: What are the four parts of the Mass? (Gathering, God’s word, Eucharist, sending forth.)
In which part do we receive Jesus? (The Eucharist.)
What does the priest say at the end? (Go in peace.)
practice: Prepare picture cards for each part of the Mass, in each of the four groups.
Mix them and have the children arrange them in order.
Play “What comes next?” Hold up a card, ask, “What comes next?” Let children answer.
Practice the responses together: “And with your spirit,” “Thanks be to God,” “Amen.”
script.close: Say together: “Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Lord, have mercy.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “At Mass, find the four parts.”

tryit: Put the parts of the Mass in order.
lessons.saintStory:
Cyril was born in about the year 313, and he became bishop of Jerusalem. It was a time when the Church was growing quickly after the persecutions ended. Many adults were learning about Jesus to be baptized at Easter.
Cyril gave talks to those who had just been baptized, explaining the Mass and the sacraments they had received. These talks, written down, are about 1,600 years old. In them he describes the prayers, the bread and wine, and how to receive Communion with reverence: “Make your left hand a throne for your right.”
Cyril shows that the Mass has been the heart of Christian life since the beginning, and that learning its parts helps us love it.

lessons.title: Mary says yes
lessons.idea: Mary said yes to God’s plan. We ask her to help us say yes. She is our mother.
lessons.question: What did Mary say at the wedding in Cana?
lessons.activity: Learn the Magnificat’s first lines. Draw Mary at Cana.
teach: Mary said yes to God (Luke 1:38; CCC 488, 494). At Cana she said, “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).
She is our mother (CCC 969). Teach the first lines of the Magnificat.
Keep Mary pointing to Jesus.
talk: How can you say yes to God?
quiz: Mary said…|Later|Let it be done to me|No|Maybe|1|Luke 1:38.
At Cana Mary said…|Wait|Go home|Be quiet|Do whatever he tells you|3|John 2:5.
Mary is our…|Friend only|Mother|Enemy|Boss|1|John 19:27.
lessons.life: Say “Yes, God” when you do a chore this week.
lessons.saint: Elizabeth, cousin of Mary: she said, “Blessed is she who believed.”
lessons.mem: My soul magnifies the Lord. (Luke 1:46)
lessons.hook: Tell about a time someone asked for your help. “What did you say?”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What did Mary say yes to?”

script.open: Say, “I need someone who is ready to say yes. Can someone help me carry this box?” Let a child say yes. “Saying yes is a wonderful thing. Mary said the most important yes of all.”
teach: Say: “When the angel Gabriel told Mary that she would be the mother of God’s Son, Mary was surprised and maybe afraid. She asked, ‘How can this be?’ And the angel said, ‘Nothing is impossible with God.’ Then Mary said, ‘Behold, I am the servant of the Lord. Let it be done to me according to your word.’ That was her yes.”

Say: “Because of Mary’s yes, Jesus came into the world. Mary was a very good mother. She helped Jesus when he was a baby, and she was there when he was dying on the cross. At Cana, when a wedding ran out of wine, Mary said to Jesus, ‘They have no wine.’ And she told the servants, ‘Do whatever he tells you.’ Jesus did a miracle. Mary always points us to Jesus.”

Read the first lines of the Magnificat: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior.” Say: “Mary sang this song when she visited Elizabeth. It means: ‘My soul tells how great God is!’ We can ask Mary to help us say yes to God, too.”
ask: What did the angel ask Mary? (To be the mother of God’s Son.)
What did Mary say? (Yes. Let it be done.)
What does Mary say to us at Cana? (Do whatever he tells you.)
practice: Teach the first lines of the Magnificat in two parts, with a clap pattern or a simple tune.
Read the story of Cana from a children’s Bible. Retell it with a pitcher and cups.
Give each child paper and crayons. Say: “Draw Mary at the wedding, telling the servants, ‘Do whatever he tells you.’”
Show and tell.
script.close: Say the Hail Mary. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Say ‘Yes, Lord’ to something hard this week.”

tryit: Learn the first lines of the Magnificat.
lessons.saintStory:
Elizabeth was the wife of a priest named Zechariah. She was old, and she and Zechariah had no children. They loved God and tried to follow him. One day an angel told Zechariah that Elizabeth would have a son, and that his name should be John.
Six months later, the angel Gabriel visited Mary, Elizabeth’s young cousin, and told her that she would be the mother of the Savior. Mary went quickly to visit Elizabeth. When Mary greeted her, the baby in Elizabeth’s womb leaped for joy. Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and said, “Blessed are you among women. Blessed is she who believed that what the Lord said to her would come true.”
Elizabeth was the first person to call Mary “mother of my Lord.” We say her words in the Hail Mary every time we pray.

lessons.title: Saints show the way
lessons.idea: Saints loved God in everyday ways. We can follow their examples.
lessons.question: Which saint do you want to be like?
lessons.activity: Create a saint “trading card” with name, feast day, a virtue and a prayer.
teach: Saints loved God in everyday ways (CCC 828, 2030). Their lives show how to follow Jesus.
Include name, feast day, a virtue and a prayer.
Choose saints from many cultures.
talk: How can you pray with your saint?
quiz: Saints show us…|How to be famous|How to follow Jesus|How to win|How to hide|1|CCC 828.
The communion of saints includes…|Only popes|All holy people|Only angels|Only monks|1|CCC 946.
We celebrate saints on…|None|Birthdays only|Feast days|Mondays|2|CCC 1173.
lessons.life: Learn the feast day of your patron saint and celebrate it.
lessons.saint: Anthony of Padua: a gifted preacher, and the friend we ask to help find lost things.
lessons.mem: Be holy, for I am holy. (1 Peter 1:16)
lessons.hook: Show baseball cards. “We make saint cards to remember heroes of faith.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to present a saint card.

script.open: Show a deck of cards, and say, “These are baseball cards (or Pokémon cards). Each one has a name, a picture, and some facts. Today, we’re going to make cards of the very best people to know: saints.”
teach: Read Hebrews 12:1-2: “Since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus.” Say: “A cloud of witnesses is a crowd of saints, cheering us on, as we run toward heaven.”

Say: “Saints are ordinary people who loved God in everyday ways. Some were kings and some were beggars. Some were children. Each of them loved Jesus, and each in their own way. We can follow the example of the saints. When we read their stories, we see what loving God looks like in real life.”

Say: “Do you have a patron saint? At Baptism, many of us are named after a saint. We can ask that saint to pray for us, and try to be like him or her. Every saint has a feast day, the day we remember them. God says in 1 Peter, ‘Be holy, for I am holy.’ That means all of us are called to be saints.”
ask: What is a saint? (A person who loved God and is in heaven.)
Who is your patron saint? (Take answers, or help children find out.)
What does God want us to be? (Holy, saints.)
practice: Give each child a blank index card.
Set up a table with books or printouts about saints. Let children choose one saint.
On the card, write or draw: the saint’s name, feast day, a virtue (like kindness, courage), and a short prayer, “Saint ___, pray for us.”
Display the cards or share them with a partner.
script.close: Say together: “Holy ones of God, pray for us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look up your patron saint with your family.”

tryit: Write the saint’s name, feast day, a virtue and a prayer.
lessons.saintStory:
Fernando was born in Lisbon, Portugal, in 1195. He became a priest, and then a Franciscan, taking the name Anthony. He wanted to be a missionary, but he got very ill, and was sent home. He was assigned to a hermitage, until one day he was asked to preach, and everyone was amazed at how well he spoke.
Anthony traveled through Italy and France, preaching about Jesus. Thousands came to hear him. He was also kind to the poor and loved to talk about the Bible. People say that a novice once took his prayer book. Anthony prayed, and the novice returned it. Since then people ask Saint Anthony to help them find things they have lost.
Anthony died young, at thirty-six. He shows how to use our gifts for God.

lessons.title: Heaven is our home
lessons.idea: Heaven is life with God forever. Jesus has prepared a place for us. We try to follow him there.
lessons.question: What do you think heaven is like?
lessons.activity: Describe heaven in a drawing without trying to “draw God.”
teach: Heaven is life with God forever (CCC 1023–1024, 1026). Jesus prepares a place for us (John 14:1–3).
Avoid boring images (clouds and harps).
Be gentle with grief; heaven is hope.
talk: What do you think heaven is like?
Who do you hope to see?
How do we get ready for heaven?
quiz: Heaven is…|A place with toys|A story|Life with God forever|A dream|2|CCC 1024.
Jesus has prepared…|Nothing|A place for us|A school|A boat|1|John 14:2.
To get to heaven, we…|Love God and others|Hide|Buy|Win|0|Matthew 25.
lessons.life: Pray for someone who has died.
lessons.saint: Bl. Chiara Badano: she said “Yes” to God even in illness.
misc: “I have to be perfect to go.”
lessons.mem: I go to prepare a place for you. (John 14:2)
lessons.hook: Say, “Imagine a home where everyone loves you.” Heaven is even better.
lessons.assess: Ask: “Who is in heaven?”

script.open: Say, “Close your eyes and think of your favorite place. Now imagine it’s a hundred times better. That’s a tiny hint of heaven.” Let them share what they imagined. “Now we’ll hear what the Bible says about heaven.”
teach: Read John 14:1-3: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself.” Say: “Jesus promised a place for us.”

Say: “Heaven is life with God forever. It is not just clouds and harps. In heaven, there is no sadness, no pain, no death. We will be with God, with Mary, the angels and the saints, and with our families who loved God. It will be the happiest place we can imagine, even happier.”

Say: “How do we get to heaven? By following Jesus: loving God and others, receiving the sacraments, praying and saying sorry when we fail. We cannot see heaven, but we can believe in it, because Jesus told us. And God invites everyone to come.”
ask: What is heaven? (Life with God forever.)
Who will be in heaven? (God, Mary, angels, saints, people who loved God.)
How can we get ready for heaven? (Follow Jesus, pray, love.)
practice: Give each child a large sheet of paper and crayons.
Say: “Draw what you imagine heaven will be like: happy, peaceful, beautiful. But don’t try to draw God. God is a mystery bigger than any picture.”
Walk around and ask each child what they included.
Hang the pictures together as a “gallery of heaven.”
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, thank you for preparing a place for us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell your family what you drew.”

tryit: Do not try to draw God.
Say: “Jesus has made a place for me.”
lessons.saintStory:
Chiara Badano was born in 1971 in a small town in northern Italy. She was a happy girl who loved tennis, swimming and singing. Her parents had waited eleven years for a child, and they called her “a gift from Mary.”
When she was sixteen, Chiara had a pain in her shoulder that would not go away. It was bone cancer. Chiara was very sick for two years. She did not want to take strong medicine, so that she could stay alert and give her pain to Jesus. She said, “If you want it, Jesus, I want it too.” Her friends visited and said they went to cheer her up, but left cheered up themselves.
Chiara died in 1990, at eighteen. She said she was going to meet Jesus, her “Bridegroom.” She shows what faith in heaven looks like.

units.title: The Ten Commandments
units.eq: How do we love God and our neighbor?

lessons.title: Love God first
lessons.idea: The first three commandments teach us to love God: worship him alone, use his name with respect, keep Sunday holy.
lessons.question: Why is God’s name holy?
lessons.activity: Match the first three commandments with actions and examples.
teach: The first three commandments: love God, respect his name, keep Sunday holy (CCC 2052, 2083, 2142, 2168).
Commandments are guides for love.
Link to prayer and Mass.
talk: Why do we use God’s name with respect?
What do we do on Sunday?
quiz: The first commandment: “I am the Lord your God. You shall have…”|No other gods before me|A king|Two gods|Many gods|0|Exodus 20:3.
Keep holy the…|Weekend|Week|Night|Lord’s Day|3|Exodus 20:8.
God’s name is…|Holy|Funny|Secret|Common|0|CCC 2142.
lessons.life: Say “Jesus” with respect and never in anger.
lessons.saint: The Martyrs of Abitinae: Christians who died rather than give up Sunday Mass.
lessons.mem: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart. (Deuteronomy 6:5)
lessons.hook: Show a family rules chart. “Rules from a loving Father.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to match each commandment with an action.

script.open: Hold up a heart cut from red paper. Say, “What goes first in your heart? Who comes first? When we have a big love, we put that person first. Today’s three commandments tell us who comes first in our hearts.”
teach: Read Exodus 20:1-11 in short pieces. Say: “These are the first three of the Ten Commandments. They are about loving God. Commandment 1: ‘I am the Lord your God. You shall have no other gods before me.’ That means God is first. Nothing and no one is more important to us than God.”

Say: “Commandment 2: ‘You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.’ God’s name is holy. We say it with love and respect. We don’t use it for a joke, or when we are angry. When we say ‘Jesus,’ it should be a prayer. Commandment 3: ‘Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.’ For Christians this is Sunday, the day of the Lord’s Resurrection. We go to Mass and rest, and spend time with family.”

Say: “Jesus said that the greatest commandment is: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind.’ The first three commandments help us do that. They show us how to put God first.”
ask: What is the first commandment about? (God comes first.)
How can we use God’s name with love? (In prayer and praise.)
Why do we keep Sunday holy? (It’s the Lord’s Day, the day Jesus rose.)
practice: Prepare three headings: “God first,” “God’s name,” “Sunday.”
Prepare action cards: “Pray in the morning,” “Say ‘Jesus’ in a prayer,” “Go to Mass,” “Ask God’s help,” “Rest and play with family,” “Don’t say ‘Oh my God’ as a joke.”
Have each child pick a card, read it with help, and put it under the right heading.
Talk about which is easy and which is hard.
script.close: Say: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Choose one thing to help you put God first this week.”

tryit: Match each commandment to an action.
Say them in your own words.
lessons.saintStory:
In the year 304, in a little town called Abitinae in North Africa, the Roman emperor Diocletian made a law. Christians were not allowed to own the Scriptures or to gather for Sunday Mass. Anyone who disobeyed could be put to death.
A group of forty-nine Christians, men, women and children, led by a priest named Saturninus, kept meeting for Mass in a private house. The Romans arrested them and took them to Carthage. When a judge asked why they had gathered, one of them said, “We cannot live without the Lord’s Day.” They would not give up Mass, even in prison, and they died for their faith.
These martyrs show us how precious the first commandments are, loving God above all, honoring his name, and keeping Sunday holy.

lessons.title: Honor your parents and respect life
lessons.idea: The next commandments teach us to honor our parents, respect life and speak the truth.
lessons.question: How can we honor our family?
lessons.activity: Make a family “thank you” poster. Role-play kind speech.
teach: Honor your father and mother (CCC 2197, 2214–2220). Do not kill; respect life (CCC 2258). Tell the truth (CCC 2464).
Honor includes thanks, care, respect.
Be sensitive about family situations.
talk: How can you honor your family?
quiz: Honor your…|Pets|Father and mother|Friends only|Teachers only|1|Exodus 20:12.
Do not…|Kill|Share|Sing|Help|0|Exodus 20:13.
Do not bear false…|Candles|Witness|Gifts|Notes|1|Exodus 20:16.
lessons.life: Thank your parents for something specific.
lessons.saint: Gianna Molla: she gave her life for her child.
lessons.mem: Honor your father and mother. (Exodus 20:12)
lessons.hook: Show photos of grandparents. “Honor means more than obey.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to name three ways to honor family.

script.open: Play a quick game of “Simon says honor.” Say, “Simon says give someone a thumbs up. Simon says say thank you.” End with “Simon says honor your father and mother.” Say, “Today we will learn what that means.”
teach: Read Exodus 20:12-16 in short pieces. Say: “These commandments are about how we treat others. Commandment 4: ‘Honor your father and your mother.’ To honor means to love, respect and obey. We do this at home and at school. This is the first commandment with a promise.”

Say: “Commandment 5: ‘You shall not kill.’ All life is a gift from God, from the smallest baby to the oldest person. We must never hurt anyone. We care for others. We protect life. Commandment 6 and 9 are about being faithful and pure in how we treat our bodies and other people. We will learn more as we grow up. Commandment 8: ‘You shall not bear false witness.’ That means we do not lie or say untrue things that hurt others.”
Say: “These commandments are God’s way of saying, ‘Treat each other with love.’ If everyone obeyed them, what would the world be like? Peaceful, happy. And we can start by obeying them ourselves.”
ask: Why do we honor our parents? (They love us and take care of us.)
Why is life so precious? (God made every person.)
What does it mean to tell the truth? (Say what’s real, not lies.)
practice: Give each family group (or each child) a sheet of poster paper.
Write across the top: “Thank you, Family!”
Let children draw their families and write one thing they are thankful for about each person.
In pairs, role-play kind words, for example, how to say, “Please stop,” without saying something mean.
script.close: Pray: “God, bless my family.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Give your thank-you poster to your family.”

tryit: Make a thank-you poster for your family.
Say one thing you are thankful for.
lessons.saintStory:
Gianna Beretta was born in Italy in 1922. She became a doctor and worked with children and mothers. She loved to ski and to hike in the mountains, and she liked to give her time to the poor and sick. She married Pietro Molla, and they had three children.
When Gianna was expecting her fourth child, the doctors found a tumor. They said she could have an operation that would end her pregnancy, but she asked them to save the baby’s life instead. She knew it was dangerous for her. She wrote to her husband, “If you must decide between me and the baby, choose the baby.”
Her daughter Gianna Emanuela was born healthy, and Gianna died a week later. She is a saint, and her daughter grew up to be a doctor too. Gianna shows what it means to respect life.

lessons.title: Be grateful and content
lessons.idea: The last commandments teach us to be pure of heart, not to steal and not to envy.
lessons.question: What do you have that you can be thankful for?
lessons.activity: Make a gratitude list and a “share with others” jar.
teach: Do not steal; do not envy; keep your heart pure (CCC 2401, 2514, 2534). Gratitude counters envy.
Share with others.
Never shame.
talk: What do you have that you can thank God for?
How do you feel when you envy?
quiz: Do not…|Share|Steal|Thank|Pray|1|Exodus 20:15.
Do not covet…|Free things|Your neighbor’s goods|Anything|Your own|1|Exodus 20:17.
Gratitude is…|Greed|Thankfulness|Envy|Anger|1|CCC 2637.
lessons.life: Write three thanks each night.
lessons.saint: Matthew: a tax collector who left his money table to follow Jesus.
lessons.mem: Give thanks in all circumstances. (1 Thessalonians 5:18)
lessons.hook: Show a jar for thank-yous. “Gratitude fills our hearts.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to list three things they are thankful for.

script.open: Put a small pile of coins on the table and say, “If I gave you all of these, what would you do with them? Would you keep them all, or share some?” Take answers. “Today’s commandments are about our things and our hearts.”
teach: Say: “Commandment 7 is, ‘You shall not steal.’ Stealing is taking something that is not yours. It is wrong, because it hurts the person and breaks trust. If we have taken something, we need to give it back and say sorry. Commandment 10 is: ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s goods.’ To covet means to be so jealous of what someone else has that we are unhappy.”

Say: “Why do we want more and more? Sometimes we think that the next toy will make us happy. But the happiest people are the grateful ones, who say thank you for what they have. St. Paul wrote, ‘Give thanks in all circumstances.’ (1 Thessalonians 5:18) Being content means being happy with what God has given us.”
Say: “God wants us to share, too. When we give to others, our hearts grow bigger. A grateful and generous heart is free from jealousy. Jesus said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”
ask: What does ‘steal’ mean? (Take something that is not yours.)
What can we do if we have taken something? (Give it back and say sorry.)
What are some things you are thankful for? (Let several share.)
practice: Give each child a sheet of paper. Say: “Make a list of ten things you are thankful for. You can draw or write.”
Decorate an empty jar or box and label it “Share Jar.”
Give each child a few slips of paper. Say: “When you share something this week, write it down and put it in the jar.”
Say a thank-you grace together.
script.close: Say the grace after meals. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Make a list of everything you’re thankful for at dinner.”

tryit: Fill a “share” jar with kind acts.
lessons.saintStory:
Matthew, also called Levi, was a tax collector in the town of Capernaum. Tax collectors were not loved. They worked for the Roman rulers, and many were known for taking more money than they should. Matthew sat at his table, counting coins.
One day Jesus walked by and said, “Follow me.” Matthew got up, left everything and followed him. He invited Jesus to dinner at his house, with many other tax collectors and sinners. Some people complained, and Jesus said, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
Matthew became one of the twelve apostles and wrote the Gospel of Matthew. He shows what it means to put God before money. Instead of grabbing, he gave everything, and found something better.

units.title: Prayer
units.eq: How do we grow close to God?

lessons.title: Our Father
lessons.idea: The Our Father is the prayer Jesus taught. It has seven requests.
lessons.question: What do we ask for in the Our Father?
lessons.activity: Illustrate each petition with a picture.
teach: Seven requests (CCC 2759, 2761, 2765). First three are about God, last four about us.
Give a simple picture for each.
Pray it together daily.
quiz: The Our Father has…|Two|Seven petitions|Ten|Twelve|1|CCC 2759.
“Give us this day our…”|Daily bread|Time|Wishes|Toys|0|Matthew 6:11.
“Deliver us from…”|Evil|Sleep|School|Work|0|Matthew 6:13.
lessons.life: Pray the Our Father slowly and think of what you are asking.
lessons.saint: Cyprian of Carthage: a bishop who wrote about the Our Father and died for Jesus.
lessons.mem: Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.
lessons.hook: Say the Our Father slowly with a gesture. “What do these words ask?”
lessons.assess: Ask children to explain one petition.

script.open: Say, “Imagine that your best friend asked you, ‘How should I talk to the king?’ What would you tell him? Now imagine the King of the Universe, and someone asked Jesus, ‘How do we talk to God?’ Jesus gave them words.”
teach: Say: “The friends of Jesus asked him, ‘Lord, teach us to pray.’ Jesus gave them the Our Father. It has seven requests, which we call petitions. Before we ask for anything, we say who we are talking to: ‘Our Father, who art in heaven.’ He is a Father who loves us.”

Go through the seven petitions: “1. Hallowed be thy name: may your name be holy. 2. Thy kingdom come: may your love rule everywhere. 3. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven: may we do what you want. 4. Give us this day our daily bread: give us what we need today. 5. Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us: forgive us, and help us forgive. 6. Lead us not into temptation: keep us from choosing wrong. 7. Deliver us from evil: keep us safe. Amen means, ‘So be it.’”
Say: “The first three ask for God’s glory. The last four ask for what we need. All together, it is the perfect prayer, because Jesus gave it to us.”
ask: Who gave us the Our Father? (Jesus.)
What do the first three petitions ask for? (That God’s name is holy, his kingdom comes and his will be done.)
What do we ask for in ‘daily bread’? (What we need each day.)
practice: Give each child a paper folded into seven boxes.
Say one petition at a time, and let each child draw a simple picture for it: hands in prayer, a crown, a heart, a loaf of bread, two people hugging, a path, a shield.
Help children write a number and a key word in each box.
Pray the Our Father together, pointing at each picture.
script.close: Pray the Our Father slowly together, with the Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray the Our Father with your family before dinner.”

tryit: Draw a picture for each part of the Our Father.
lessons.saintStory:
Cyprian was born around the year 200 in Carthage, in North Africa. He was a wealthy teacher of speech who became a Christian when he was an adult. He gave his money to the poor and was chosen as bishop.
In those days Christians were often put in prison. Cyprian cared for the Church through plagues and persecution, leading the people and writing letters to comfort them. He wrote a famous little book about the Our Father, in which he explained each line. He wrote that Jesus himself gave us this prayer, so it is the best way to talk to the Father.
In 258 Cyprian was arrested and condemned. When the judge read the sentence, Cyprian said, “Thanks be to God.” He died as a martyr. He shows us the power of the Our Father.

lessons.title: Prayers of the Church
lessons.idea: We pray the Hail Mary, Glory Be, Apostles’ Creed and Act of Contrition. We memorize them to pray anywhere.
lessons.question: Which prayer do you know by heart?
lessons.activity: Play a memory game with the basic prayers.
teach: The Hail Mary, Glory Be, Apostles’ Creed and Act of Contrition are prayers of the Church (CCC 2676, 2698).
Repeat and review often.
Prayer is relationship, not performance.
talk: Which prayer do you know by heart?
quiz: The Apostles’ Creed begins…|I believe in God|Glory be|Hail Mary|Our Father|0|CCC 194.
The Glory Be praises…|Mary|The Trinity|Saints|Angels|1|CCC 2639.
The Act of Contrition expresses…|Anger|Joy|Fear|Sorrow|3|CCC 1451.
lessons.life: Learn one new prayer each week.
lessons.saint: Zélie Martin: a mother who taught her children to pray.
lessons.mem: Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.
lessons.hook: Play a memory game with prayer cards.
lessons.assess: Ask children to say a prayer they know by heart.

script.open: Say the first line of the Sign of the Cross, then stop. Let the children finish it. Then do the first line of the Our Father, then the Hail Mary. Say, “Look! You know so many prayers already. That is a treasure. Today we are going to learn even more, so we can pray anywhere, anytime.”
teach: Say: “There are some prayers that every Catholic knows by heart. The Sign of the Cross begins them all. The Our Father is the prayer Jesus taught. The Hail Mary is Mary’s prayer. The Glory Be praises the Trinity. The Apostles’ Creed says what we believe. And the Act of Contrition says sorry.”

Say the Apostles’ Creed in pieces: “I believe in God the Father almighty. I believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord. He suffered, died and rose. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Catholic Church, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body and life everlasting.” Say: “A creed is a statement of what we believe. We say it at Mass on Sundays.”

Say: “Why do we learn these prayers by heart? So that we can pray anywhere. When we are in the car, at school, in the dark, we can still talk to God. These prayers also connect us to all other Catholics around the world, who say the same prayers. Praying by heart is like carrying a treasure in your heart.”
ask: What are some prayers every Catholic knows? (Sign of the Cross, Our Father, Hail Mary, Glory Be.)
What does the Creed say? (What we believe.)
Why is it good to know prayers by heart? (We can pray anywhere.)
practice: Make a set of cards: for each prayer, one card with the opening words (“Our Father who art…”) and one with the ending (“…deliver us from evil. Amen.”).
Mix the cards, spread them face down, and play a memory game. Children flip two cards and see if they match.
When a pair matches, say the whole line together.
End by reciting the Glory Be by heart.
script.close: Say the Glory Be by heart. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray one of our prayers with your family tonight.”

tryit: Play a memory game with the prayers.
Match the prayers’ openings and endings.
lessons.saintStory:
Zélie Guérin was born in France in 1831. She wanted to be a nun, but she was told that she was not called to it, so she became a lacemaker. She married Louis Martin, a watchmaker, and they had nine children. Four of them died young, which was a very great sorrow.
Zélie and Louis prayed with their children every morning and evening. They went to Mass every day, and they taught the children to say their prayers, say sorry, and help the poor. Their youngest daughter, Thérèse, became a saint. Zélie died of cancer at forty-five.
Zélie and Louis were named saints together in 2015, the first married couple canonized together. They show that a family can become holy, and that learning prayers at home is the way we begin.

lessons.title: Quiet time with God
lessons.idea: We can pray in silence and listen to God. This is meditation.
lessons.question: What can you hear when it is quiet?
lessons.activity: Practice a minute of silence. Take turns saying, “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.”
teach: Meditation is quiet listening (Psalm 46:10; CCC 2705, 2708, 2710). Samuel heard God’s voice (1 Samuel 3:1–10).
Start with 30 seconds.
No pressure.
talk: What can you hear when it’s quiet?
What do you want to say to God?
quiz: Meditation is…|Noise|Sleep|Exercise|Quiet prayer|3|CCC 2705.
Samuel said…|Go away|No|Speak, Lord|Later|2|1 Samuel 3:10.
God listens…|Only at church|Always|Never|Sometimes|1|Psalm 34:15.
lessons.life: Spend one minute in silence each day.
lessons.saint: Mary: she kept everything in her heart and thought about it.
lessons.mem: Speak, Lord, your servant is listening. (1 Samuel 3:9)
lessons.hook: Ask for silence for ten seconds. “What do you hear?”
lessons.assess: Ask children to be quiet for one minute and share one thing.

script.open: Ring a small bell and say, “Listen. Keep listening until you can’t hear the bell anymore. Then raise your hand.” Wait for the sound to fade. “That’s what listening feels like. God wants to speak to us, and we can listen.”
teach: Say: “Prayer is not only talking. It is also listening. The Bible says in Psalm 46, ‘Be still, and know that I am God.’ To be still means to be quiet and calm. This is called silent prayer or meditation. We don’t need many words. We just sit with God, like sitting next to a friend.”

Tell 1 Samuel 3:1-10: “A boy named Samuel slept in the temple. In the night he heard a voice calling, ‘Samuel!’ He ran to the priest Eli, ‘Here I am.’ But Eli said, ‘I didn’t call you.’ This happened three times. Eli realized that it was God, and told Samuel, ‘Go back to bed. If he calls again, say, “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.”’ Samuel did, and God spoke to him.”

Say: “God still speaks to us. Not usually in a loud voice, but in our hearts. We listen by being quiet, and by paying attention to the Bible, our conscience and the people who love us. You can say, ‘Speak, Lord, your servant is listening,’ any time.”
ask: What did Samuel say? (Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.)
How do we listen to God? (In silence, in the Bible, in our heart.)
What is it like to be quiet with God? (Peaceful, calm. Take answers.)
practice: Light a candle, and sit in a circle on the floor.
Say: “We will be quiet for one minute. Close your eyes and say in your heart, ‘Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.’” Keep time.
Then pass a small object around the circle. Each child who holds it says the prayer aloud: “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.”
End with a quiet “Amen.”
script.close: Pray quietly: “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Be quiet with God for one minute before bed.”

tryit: Take turns saying: “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.”
lessons.saintStory:
After the shepherds left the stable, the Bible says, “Mary kept all these things, pondering them in her heart.” To ponder means to think about something slowly and deeply, as you turn it over in your mind.
Mary pondered the angel’s words and the shepherds’ visit. She pondered when Jesus was twelve and stayed behind in the Temple. She did not understand everything, but she kept thinking and praying. The Gospel says again and again that Mary kept things in her heart.
Mary teaches us to be quiet and listen to God, to remember what he has done and to pray about it. She is a model for quiet prayer.

units.title: The Church year
units.eq: How does the Church help us follow Jesus all year?

lessons.title: Advent and Christmas
lessons.idea: We prepare for Jesus’ birth and then celebrate it for many days.
lessons.question: What do we do in Advent to prepare?
lessons.activity: Create an Advent calendar with acts of love.
teach: Advent prepares for Christmas; Christmas lasts to the Baptism of the Lord (CCC 524–525, 1171).
Do acts of kindness.
Keep the season distinct.
talk: How can you prepare your heart?
quiz: Advent lasts about…|Four weeks|Ten days|One week|Two months|0|CCC 524.
Advent candles are…|Red|Purple and pink|Gold|Blue|1|Liturgy.
We wait for…|Jesus|A party|A gift only|A trip|0|CCC 524.
lessons.life: Do one act of kindness each day in Advent.
lessons.saint: Mary and Joseph: they prepared for Jesus’ birth and welcomed him.
lessons.mem: Come, Lord Jesus.
lessons.hook: Light the wreath. “We prepare our hearts.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to name one Advent practice.

script.open: Show a paper-chain countdown or a regular calendar. Ask, “Have you ever counted days until something special? How did you wait?” Then say, “Advent is a time of waiting, with joy.”
teach: Say: “Advent means ‘coming.’ It is the four weeks before Christmas. The Church’s year begins with Advent. We wait for Jesus to come, and we get ready. The color is purple, a sign of preparing. We light candles on the Advent wreath, one more each week. On the third Sunday the candle is pink, for joy: the waiting is almost over.”

Say: “We are waiting for Jesus in three ways. We remember how he came as a baby in Bethlehem. We open our hearts to him now, every day. And we look forward to when he will come again at the end of time. That’s why we say, ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’”

Say: “How do we get ready? We pray each day. We say sorry for our sins. We do kind acts. We share with people who need help. We make our hearts like a clean, warm stable for Jesus. Mary and Joseph got ready, too, and they welcomed him with love.”
ask: What does ‘Advent’ mean? (Coming.)
How many weeks is Advent? (Four.)
